transcript: I always love when weird, quirky off Broadway musicals come to Broadway, and so when Dead Outlaw announced that it was transferring, I was really excited. I had seen the show off Broadway and absolutely loved the score. I think it is probably the best score that David Yasbeck has written, and the story is absolutely wild and 100% true. It tells the story of an outlaw who achieves so much more success in death than he ever did in life. And I'm happy to say that all of that charm that it had off Broadway is definitely retained in this Broadway transfer. In fact, it's almost to its detriment, as while there are a few noticeable set upgrades, for the most part they really didn't do much to scale up the presentation of the show. And while I never thought it hindered the storytelling, it was just a little bit disappointing to see that they couldn't do more with a Broadway budget. The one area where it got a massive upgrade is in the lighting. The lighting in the show is incredible and often emulates concert lighting at times, giving the whole show a big party vibe, which I realize is a weird thing to say about a show about death. While there are some more somber moments, for the most part this show is a comedic look at this man's life and death. They actually think that tone works really well given the absurdity of the story at Times and the performances are great across the board. Of course. Shout out to Andrew Durand, who not only does a great job playing Elmer, our dead outlaw, when he is alive, but also literally just stands in a coffin for 40 minutes as he plays him while he's dead. I would definitely recommend Dead Outlaw. It's definitely quirky and off beat. It's very different from what you normally find on Broadway, but I also think that's largely what makes it unique and special.
